Q: Is Borland C++ not C++? A:

It is both. Borland C++ 3.0 is a product that ships two separate compilers — an ANSI C (C89) compiler and a C++ compiler — inside one IDE and one command-line driver. Which one runs is decided by the file extension of your source file:

ExtensionCompiler used.cC compiler (ANSI C / K&R).cppC++ compiler

So if you name your file hello.c, you are writing C. Name it hello.cpp and you are writing C++. Nothing is "mixed up" — you have simply been using the C half of a C/C++ product.

Why the confusing names

Borland's DOS compiler line evolved, and the old names stuck in classrooms:

  • Turbo C 1.0–2.0 (1987–1989) — C only, no C++ support.

  • Turbo C++ 1.0 (May 1990) — Turbo C and C++ folded into a single product; the name "Turbo C" was retired after 2.0.

  • Borland C++ 3.x (1991–1992) — the professional-tier version of the same technology; ships the C compiler, the C++ compiler, and Turbo Assembler.

Because each release stayed backward compatible with the last, people kept saying "Turbo C" long after the product on their disk was actually Turbo C++ or Borland C++. Your course is almost certainly doing the same thing.

How to tell which mode you are in

Compile this two-line program:

c

int new;

int main(void) { return 0; }

  • It compiles → you are in C mode (new is an ordinary identifier).

  • It fails → you are in C++ mode (new is a reserved keyword).

Other quick tells for C++ mode: // comments alone are not proof (Borland's C compiler accepts them too), but declaring a class, overloading a function, or using bool will only work in C++.

You can also force the choice explicitly with the -P command-line switch on bcc: -P compiles everything as C++ regardless of extension, -P- compiles as C.

What standards you are actually targeting

  • C side: ANSI C, i.e. C89/C90. No C99 features — no //-guaranteed portability, no declarations mid-block, no long long, no <stdint.h>, no variable-length arrays.

  • C++ side: roughly AT&T cfront 2.1 compatibility in 3.0 (3.1 claims 3.0). This is pre-standard C++ — years before C++98. No namespaces, no bool, no exceptions worth relying on, no STL, no templates you should trust, and headers are <iostream.h> rather than <iostream>.

  • Plus non-standard DOS extensions: <conio.h> (clrscr(), getch()), <dos.h>, <graphics.h>, inline asm blocks, and the near/far/huge memory-model pointer keywords.

That last group is the practical trap: code you write in this environment often will not compile anywhere else, and code you find on the web (written for modern compilers) often will not compile here.

Why C code "just works" in a C++ compiler anyway

Even setting the two-compilers fact aside, C and C++ share a large common subset, so most simple C programs compile as C++ with few or no edits. But this is not a guarantee — C++ is stricter and differs in real ways:

c

int *p = malloc(n);   /* fine in C, error in C++ — needs an explicit cast */
char *s = "hello";    /* fine in C, deprecated/ill-formed in modern C++ */
int class;            /* fine in C, error in C++ — reserved word */

So "it compiled, therefore it's C++" is not a safe inference, and neither is the reverse.

Practical advice

If you are learning today, this toolchain is roughly 35 years old and teaches habits (DOS-only headers, pre-standard C++, 16-bit memory models) that you will have to unlearn. If you have a choice, use a current compiler — GCC, Clang, or MSVC are all free and standards-conforming. If your course mandates a DOS environment, DJGPP is a free, modern GCC port for DOS. If your course mandates Borland specifically, run it under DOSBox and treat everything outside the standard library as course-specific trivia rather than as C or C++ knowledge.

Bottom line: Borland C++ 3.0 is a real C++ compiler — and also a real C compiler. Your .c files have been going through the C one.

Q: What is bold text? WCAG contrast requirements SC 1.4.3 A:

Automatic accessibility audits have their limits, and auditors should know that. They are supposed to audit conformance with the WCAG, not with their test tool. That’s why audits are manual to begin with.

The logic would be: If you let criterion 1.4.3 pass for Open Sans Bold, you should let it pass for Lato Regular as well, as the rendered font weight is at least as heavy.

WCAG

As you correctly mention, WCAG 2.2’s criterion 1.4.3 makes an exception for Large Text (14pt bold), in that a lower contrast is required:

Large-scale text […] have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1;

Large scale text is in turn defined as:

[…] with at least […] 14 point bold

The WCAG don’t mention how to determine if text is bold.

ACT Rules

When looking at the Rules for Accessibility Conformance Testing (ACT) regarding 1.4.3, there is another definition for Large Scale Text:

Large Scale Text

A text node is large scale text if at least one of the following is true:

  • the text node computed font-size is at least 14 points and has a computed font weight of 700 or higher.

Here, the rule would actually rely on the calculated styles and specifically font-size and font-weight.

But then again, the ACT rules are not normative, only informative.

While they help cover most cases, an auditor should let the criterion pass when confronted with evidence like rendered text in a screenshot. If they are rigid and blindly rely on their tools, one could hack around it by changing the font-face definition:

@font-face {
  font-family: "Lato Regular";
  font-weight: 700;
  src: url(/* Source of the regular lato font face */);
}

some-selector {
  font-family: "Lato Regular";
  font-weight: 700;
}
